# AllocProfiler in divan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/divan/0.1.21/divan/struct.AllocProfiler.html

`pub struct AllocProfiler<Alloc = `[System](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/alloc/struct.System.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

Measures [ GlobalAlloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/alloc/global/trait.GlobalAlloc.html) memory usage.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The default usage is to create a
[ #[global_allocator]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macros/builtin/attr.global_allocator.html) that wraps the

[allocator with](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/alloc/struct.System.html)

`System`[:](https://docs.rs/struct.AllocProfiler.html#method.system)

`AllocProfiler::system()````
use std::collections::*;
use divan::AllocProfiler;
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: AllocProfiler = AllocProfiler::system();
fn main() {
    divan::main();
}
#[divan::bench(types = [
    Vec<i32>,
    LinkedList<i32>,
    HashSet<i32>,
])]
fn from_iter<T>() -> T
where
    T: FromIterator<i32>,
{
    (0..100).collect()
}
#[divan::bench(types = [
    Vec<i32>,
    LinkedList<i32>,
    HashSet<i32>,
])]
fn drop<T>(bencher: divan::Bencher)
where
    T: FromIterator<i32>,
{
    bencher
        .with_inputs(|| (0..100).collect::<T>())
        .bench_values(std::mem::drop);
}
```
Wrap other [ GlobalAlloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/alloc/global/trait.GlobalAlloc.html) implementations like

[with](https://docs.rs/mimalloc)

`mimalloc`[:](https://docs.rs/struct.AllocProfiler.html#method.new)

`AllocProfiler::new()````
use divan::AllocProfiler;
use mimalloc::MiMalloc;
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: AllocProfiler<MiMalloc> = AllocProfiler::new(MiMalloc);
```
See [ string](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/blob/main/examples/benches/string.rs)
and

[benchmarks for more examples.](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/blob/main/examples/benches/collections.rs)

`collections`[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

Collecting allocation information happens at any point during which Divan is also measuring the time. As a result, counting allocations affects timing.

To reduce Divan’s footprint during benchmarking:

- Allocation information is recorded in thread-local storage to prevent
contention when benchmarks involve multiple threads, either through
options like `threads`
- It does not check for overflow and assumes it will not happen. This is subject to change in the future.
- Fast thread-local storage access is assembly-optimized on macOS.

Allocation information is the only data Divan records outside of timing, and thus it also has the only code that affects timing. Steps for recording alloc info:

-
Load the thread-local slot for allocation information. On macOS, this is via the `gs``tpidrro_el0``pthread_getspecific``thread_local!`
-
Increment allocation operation invocation count and bytes count (a.k.a. size).

Allocation information is recorded in thread-local storage to prevent
slowdowns from synchronized sharing when using multiple threads, through
options like [ threads](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#threads).

Note that allocations in threads not controlled by Divan are not currently counted.

# Bencher in divan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/divan/0.1.21/divan/struct.Bencher.html

`pub struct Bencher<'a, 'b, C = BencherConfig> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Enables contextual benchmarking in [ #[divan::bench]](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use divan::{Bencher, black_box};
#[divan::bench]
fn copy_from_slice(bencher: Bencher) {
    // Input and output buffers get used in the closure.
    let src = (0..100).collect::<Vec<i32>>();
    let mut dst = vec![0; src.len()];
    bencher.bench_local(|| {
        black_box(&mut dst).copy_from_slice(black_box(&src));
    });
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Benchmarks a function.

The function can be benchmarked in parallel using the [ threads
option](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#threads). If the function is strictly
single-threaded, use

[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.bench_local)

`Bencher::bench_local`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
#[divan::bench]
fn bench(bencher: divan::Bencher) {
    bencher.bench(|| {
        // Benchmarked code...
    });
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/divan/benchmark/mod.rs.html#157-159)#### pub fn [with_inputs](https://docs.rs#method.with_inputs)<G>(self, gen_input: G) -> [Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html)<'a, 'b, BencherConfig<G>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/divan/benchmark/mod.rs.html#157-159)

#### pub fn [with_inputs](https://docs.rs#method.with_inputs)<G>(self, gen_input: G) -> [Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html)<'a, 'b, BencherConfig<G>>

Generate inputs for the [benchmarked function](https://docs.rs#input-bench).

Time spent generating inputs does not affect benchmark timing.

When [benchmarking in parallel](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#threads), the input
generator is called on the same thread as the sample loop that uses that
input.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
#[divan::bench]
fn bench(bencher: divan::Bencher) {
    bencher
        .with_inputs(|| {
            // Generate input:
            String::from("...")
        })
        .bench_values(|s| {
            // Use input by-value:
            s + "123"
        });
}
```
Assign a [ Counter](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html) for all iterations of the benchmarked function.

This will either:

- Assign a new counter
- Override an existing counter of the same type

If the counter depends on [generated inputs](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.with_inputs), use
[ Bencher::input_counter](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.input_counter) instead.

If context is not needed, the counter can instead be set via
[ #[divan::bench(counters = ...)]](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#counters).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use divan::{Bencher, counter::BytesCount};
#[divan::bench]
fn char_count(bencher: Bencher) {
    let s: String = // ...
    bencher
        .counter(BytesCount::of_str(&s))
        .bench(|| {
            divan::black_box(&s).chars().count()
        });
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/divan/benchmark/mod.rs.html#244-251)#### pub fn [input_counter](https://docs.rs#method.input_counter)<C, F>(self, make_counter: F) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/divan/benchmark/mod.rs.html#244-251)

#### pub fn [input_counter](https://docs.rs#method.input_counter)<C, F>(self, make_counter: F) -> Self

Calls a closure to create a [ Counter](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html) for each input of the
benchmarked function.

This will either:

- Assign a new counter
- Override an existing counter of the same type

If the counter is constant, use [ Bencher::counter](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.counter) instead.

When [benchmarking in parallel](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#threads), the input
counter is called on the same thread as the sample loop that generates
and uses that input.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

The following example emits info for the number of bytes processed when
benchmarking [ char-counting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.Chars.html#method.count). The byte count
is gotten by calling

[on each iteration’s input](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.BytesCount.html#method.of_str)

`BytesCount::of_str`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````

# black_box in divan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/divan/0.1.21/divan/fn.black_box.html

`pub const fn black_box<T>(dummy: T) -> T`## Expand description

Prevents compiler optimizations on a value.

`black_box` should only be used on [inputs](https://docs.rs#benchmark-inputs) and
[outputs](https://docs.rs#benchmark-outputs) of benchmarks. Newcomers to benchmarking may
be tempted to also use `black_box` within the implementation, but doing so
will overly pessimize the measured code without any benefit.

[§](https://docs.rs#benchmark-inputs)Benchmark Inputs

When benchmarking, it’s good practice to ensure measurements are accurate by preventing the compiler from optimizing based on assumptions about benchmark inputs.

The compiler can optimize code for indices it knows about, such as by removing bounds checks or unrolling loops. If real-world use of your code would not know indices up front, consider preventing optimizations on them in benchmarks:

```
use divan::black_box;
const INDEX: usize = // ...
const SLICE: &[u8] = // ...
#[divan::bench]
fn bench() {
    work(&SLICE[black_box(INDEX)..]);
}
```
The compiler may also optimize for the data itself, which can also be
avoided with `black_box`:

```
#[divan::bench]
fn bench() {
    work(black_box(&SLICE[black_box(INDEX)..]));
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#benchmark-outputs)Benchmark Outputs

When benchmarking, it’s best to ensure that all of the code is actually being run. If the compiler knows an output is unused, it may remove the code that generated the output. This optimization can make benchmarks appear much faster than they really are.

At the end of a benchmark, we can force the compiler to treat outputs as if they were actually used:

```
#[divan::bench]
fn bench() {
    black_box(value.to_string());
}
```
To make the code clearer to readers that the output is discarded, this code
could instead call [ black_box_drop](https://docs.rs/fn.black_box_drop.html).

Alternatively, the output can be returned from the benchmark:

```
#[divan::bench]
fn bench() -> String {
    value.to_string()
}
```
Returning the output will `black_box` it and also avoid measuring the time
to [drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html) the output, which in this case is the time to deallocate a
[ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html). Read more about this in the

[.](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#drop)

`#[divan::bench]`
docs# Standard Library Documentation

An identity function that * hints* to the compiler to be maximally pessimistic about what

`black_box` could do.Unlike [ std::convert::identity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/fn.identity.html), a Rust compiler is encouraged to assume that

`black_box` can
use `dummy` in any possible valid way that Rust code is allowed to without introducing undefined
behavior in the calling code. This property makes `black_box` useful for writing code in which
certain optimizations are not desired, such as benchmarks.Note however, that `black_box` is only (and can only be) provided on a “best-effort” basis. The
extent to which it can block optimisations may vary depending upon the platform and code-gen
backend used. Programs cannot rely on `black_box` for *correctness*, beyond it behaving as the
identity function. As such, it **must not be relied upon to control critical program behavior.**
This also means that this function does not offer any guarantees for cryptographic or security
purposes.

This limitation is not specific to `black_box`; there is no mechanism in the entire Rust
language that can provide the guarantees required for constant-time cryptography.
(There is also no such mechanism in LLVM, so the same is true for every other LLVM-based compiler.)

[§](https://docs.rs#when-is-this-useful)When is this useful?

While not suitable in those mission-critical cases, `black_box`’s functionality can generally be
relied upon for benchmarking, and should be used there. It will try to ensure that the
compiler doesn’t optimize away part of the intended test code based on context. For
example:

```
fn contains(haystack: &[&str], needle: &str) -> bool {
    haystack.iter().any(|x| x == &needle)
}
pub fn benchmark() {
    let haystack = vec!["abc", "def", "ghi", "jkl", "mno"];
    let needle = "ghi";
    for _ in 0..10 {
        contains(&haystack, needle);
    }
}
```
The compiler could theoretically make optimizations like the following:

- The `needle`and`haystack`do not change, move the call to`contains`outside the loop and delete the loop
- Inline `contains`
- `needle`and- `haystack`have values known at compile time,- `contains`is always true. Remove the call and replace with- `true`
- Nothing is done with the result of `contains`: delete this function call entirely
- `benchmark`now has no purpose: delete this function

It is not likely that all of the above happens, but the compiler is definitely able to make some
optimizations that could result in a very inaccurate benchmark. This is where `black_box` comes
in:

```
use std::hint::black_box;
// Same `contains` function.
fn contains(haystack: &[&str], needle: &str) -> bool {
    haystack.iter().any(|x| x == &needle)
}
pub fn benchmark() {
    let haystack = vec!["abc", "def", "ghi", "jkl", "mno"];
    let needle = "ghi";
    for _ in 0..10 {
        // Force the compiler to run `contains`, even though it is a pure function whose
        // results are unused.
        black_box(contains(
            // Prevent the compiler from making assumptions about the input.
            black_box(&haystack),
            black_box(needle),
        ));
    }
}
```
This essentially tells the compiler to block optimizations across any calls to `black_box`. So,
it now:

- Treats both arguments to `contains`as unpredictable: the body of`contains`can no longer be optimized based on argument values
- Treats the call to `contains`and its result as volatile: the body of`benchmark`cannot optimize this away

This makes our benchmark much more realistic to how the function would actually be used, where arguments are usually not known at compile time and the result is used in some way.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-this)How to use this

In practice, `black_box` serves two purposes:

- It prevents the compiler from making optimizations related to the value returned by `black_box`
- It forces the value passed to `black_box`to be calculated, even if the return value of`black_box`is unused

```
use std::hint::black_box;
let zero = 0;
let five = 5;
// The compiler will see this and remove the `* five` call, because it knows that multiplying
// any integer by 0 will result in 0.
let c = zero * five;
// Adding `black_box` here disables the compiler's ability to reason about the first operand in the multiplication.
// It is forced to assume that it can be any possible number, so it cannot remove the `* five`
// operation.
let c = black_box(zero) * five;
```
While most cases will not be as clear-cut as the above example, it still illustrates how
`black_box` can be used. When benchmarking a function, you usually want to wrap its inputs in
`black_box` so the compiler cannot make optimizations that would be unrealistic in real-life
use.

```
use std::hint::black_box;
// This is a simple function that increments its input by 1. Note that it is pure, meaning it
// has no side-effects. This function has no effect if its result is unused. (An example of a
// function *with* side-effects is `println!()`.)
fn increment(x: u8) -> u8 {
    x + 1
}
// Here, we call `increment` but discard its result. The compiler, seeing this and knowing that
// `increment` is pure, will eliminate this function call entirely. This may not be desired,
// though, especially if we're trying to track how much time `increment` takes to execute.
let _ = increment(black_box(5));
// Here, we force `increment` to be executed. This is because the compiler treats `black_box`
// as if it has side-effects, and thus must compute its input.
let _ = black_box(increment(black_box(5)));
```
There may be additional situations where you want to wrap the result of a function in
`black_box` to force its execution. This is situational though, and may not have any effect
(such as when the function returns a zero-sized type such as [ () unit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)).

Note that `black_box` has no effect on how its input is treated, only its output. As such,
expressions passed to `black_box` may still be optimized:

```
use std::hint::black_box;
// The compiler sees this...
let y = black_box(5 * 10);
// ...as this. As such, it will likely simplify `5 * 10` to just `50`.
let _0 = 5 * 10;
let y = black_box(_0);
```
In the above example, the `5 * 10` expression is considered distinct from the `black_box` call,
and thus is still optimized by the compiler. You can prevent this by moving the multiplication
operation outside of `black_box`:

```
use std::hint::black_box;
// No assumptions can be made about either operand, so the multiplication is not optimized out.
let y = black_box(5) * black_box(10);
```
During constant evaluation, `black_box` is treated as a no-op.

# Function black_box_drop

[Source](../src/divan/lib.rs.html#183-185) `pub fn black_box_drop<T>(dummy: T)`

## Expand description

`black_box``drop`

[§](#examples)Examples

This is useful when benchmarking a lazy `Iterator``for_each`

```
#[divan::bench]
fn parse_iter() {
    let input: &str = Parser::new(input)
        .for_each(divan::black_box_drop);
}
```

# bench_group in divan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/divan/0.1.21/divan/attr.bench_group.html

`#[bench_group]`## Expand description

Registers a benchmarking group.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This is used for setting [options](https://docs.rs#options) shared across
[ #[divan::bench]](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html) functions in the same module:

```
#[divan::bench_group(
    sample_count = 100,
    sample_size = 500,
)]
mod math {
    use divan::black_box;
    #[divan::bench]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        black_box(1) + black_box(42)
    }
    #[divan::bench]
    fn div() -> i32 {
        black_box(1) / black_box(42)
    }
}
fn main() {
    // Run `math::add` and `math::div` benchmarks:
    divan::main();
}
```
Benchmarking [options](https://docs.rs#options) set on parent groups cascade into child groups and
their benchmarks:

```
#[divan::bench_group(
    sample_count = 100,
    sample_size = 500,
)]
mod parent {
    #[divan::bench_group(sample_size = 1)]
    mod child1 {
        #[divan::bench]
        fn bench() {
            // Will be sampled 100 times with 1 iteration per sample.
        }
    }
    #[divan::bench_group(sample_count = 42)]
    mod child2 {
        #[divan::bench]
        fn bench() {
            // Will be sampled 42 times with 500 iterations per sample.
        }
    }
    mod child3 {
        #[divan::bench(sample_count = 1)]
        fn bench() {
            // Will be sampled 1 time with 500 iterations per sample.
        }
    }
}
```
Applying this attribute multiple times to the same item will cause a compile error:

[§](https://docs.rs#options)Options

[§](https://docs.rs#name)`name`

By default, the benchmark group uses the module’s name. It can be overridden
via the `name` option:

```
#[divan::bench_group(name = "my_math")]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench(name = "my_add")]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        // Will appear as "crate_name::my_math::my_add".
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate)`crate`

The path to the specific `divan` crate instance used by this macro’s
generated code can be specified via the [ crate](https://docs.rs#crate) option. This is applicable
when using

`divan` via a macro from your own crate.```
extern crate divan as sofa;
#[::sofa::bench_group(crate = ::sofa)]
mod math {
    #[::sofa::bench(crate = ::sofa)]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        // ...
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#sample_count)`sample_count`

The number of statistical sample recordings can be set to a predetermined
[ u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) value via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#sample_count)

`sample_count``DIVAN_SAMPLE_COUNT` environment variable or
`--sample-count` CLI argument.```
#[divan::bench_group(sample_count = 1000)]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        // ...
    }
}
```
If the [ threads](https://docs.rs#threads) option is enabled, sample count becomes a multiple of the
number of threads. This is because each thread operates over the same sample
size to ensure there are always N competing threads doing the same amount of
work.

[§](https://docs.rs#sample_size)`sample_size`

The number iterations within each statistical sample can be set to a
predetermined [ u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) value via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#sample_size)

`sample_size``DIVAN_SAMPLE_SIZE` environment
variable or `--sample-size` CLI argument.```
#[divan::bench_group(sample_size = 1000)]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        // ...
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#threads)`threads`

See [ #[divan::bench(threads = ...)]](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#threads).

[§](https://docs.rs#counters)`counters`

The [ Counters](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html) of each iteration of benchmarked
functions in a group can be set via the

[option. The following example emits info for the number of bytes and number of ints processed when benchmarking](https://docs.rs#counters)

`counters`[slice sorting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.sort):

```
use divan::{Bencher, counter::{BytesCount, ItemsCount}};
const INTS: &[i32] = &[
    // ...
];
#[divan::bench_group(counters = [
    BytesCount::of_slice(INTS),
    ItemsCount::new(INTS.len()),
])]
mod sort {
    use super::*;
    #[divan::bench]
    fn default(bencher: Bencher) {
        bencher
            .with_inputs(|| INTS.to_vec())
            .bench_refs(|ints| ints.sort());
    }
    #[divan::bench]
    fn unstable(bencher: Bencher) {
        bencher
            .with_inputs(|| INTS.to_vec())
            .bench_refs(|ints| ints.sort_unstable());
    }
}
```
For convenience, singular `counter` allows a single
[ Counter](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html) to be set. The following example emits
info for the number of bytes processed when benchmarking

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.Chars.html#method.count)

`char`-counting[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.Chars.html#method.collect)

`char`-collecting```
use divan::counter::BytesCount;
const STR: &str = "...";
#[divan::bench_group(counter = BytesCount::of_str(STR))]
mod chars {
    use super::STR;
    #[divan::bench]
    fn count() -> usize {
        divan::black_box(STR).chars().count()
    }
    #[divan::bench]
    fn collect() -> String {
        divan::black_box(STR).chars().collect()
    }
}
```
See:

[§](https://docs.rs#bytes_count)`bytes_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [BytesCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.BytesCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#chars_count)`chars_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [CharsCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.CharsCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#cycles_count)`cycles_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [CyclesCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.CyclesCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#items_count)`items_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [ItemsCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.ItemsCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#min_time)`min_time`

The minimum time spent benchmarking each function can be set to a
predetermined [ Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html) via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#min_time)

`min_time``DIVAN_MIN_TIME` environment variable
or `--min-time` CLI argument.Unless [ skip_ext_time](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time) is set, this includes time external to benchmarked
functions, such as time spent generating inputs and running

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop````
use std::time::Duration;
#[divan::bench_group(min_time = Duration::from_secs(3))]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        // ...
    }
}
```
For convenience, [ min_time](https://docs.rs#min_time) can also be set with seconds as

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)

`u64`[. Invalid values will cause a panic at runtime.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64````
#[divan::bench_group(min_time = 2)]
mod int_secs {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench_group(min_time = 1.5)]
mod float_secs {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#max_time)`max_time`

The maximum time spent benchmarking each function can be set to a
predetermined [ Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html) via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#max_time)

`max_time``DIVAN_MAX_TIME` environment variable
or `--max-time` CLI argument.Unless [ skip_ext_time](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time) is set, this includes time external to benchmarked
functions, such as time spent generating inputs and running

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`If `min_time > max_time`, then [ max_time](https://docs.rs#max_time) has priority and

[will not be reached.](https://docs.rs#min_time)

`min_time````
use std::time::Duration;
#[divan::bench_group(max_time = Duration::from_secs(5))]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench]
    fn add() -> i32 {
        // ...
    }
}
```
For convenience, like [ min_time](https://docs.rs#min_time),

[can also be set with seconds as](https://docs.rs#max_time)

`max_time`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)

`u64`[. Invalid values will cause a panic at runtime.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64````
#[divan::bench_group(max_time = 8)]
mod int_secs {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench_group(max_time = 9.5)]
mod float_secs {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time)`skip_ext_time`

By default, [ min_time](https://docs.rs#min_time) and

[include time external to benchmarked functions, such as time spent generating inputs and running](https://docs.rs#max_time)

`max_time`[. Enabling the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[option will instead make those options only consider time spent within benchmarked functions. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time)

`skip_ext_time``DIVAN_SKIP_EXT_TIME` environment
variable or `--skip-ext-time` CLI argument.In the following example, [ max_time](https://docs.rs#max_time) only considers time spent running

`measured_function`:```
#[divan::bench_group(skip_ext_time)]
mod group {
    #[divan::bench(max_time = 5)]
    fn bench(bencher: divan::Bencher) {
        bencher
            .with_inputs(|| generate_input())
            .bench_values(|input| measured_function(input));
    }
}
```
This option can be set to an explicit [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) value to override parent
values:

```
#[divan::bench_group(skip_ext_time = false)]
mod group {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#ignore)`ignore`

Like [ #[test]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/testing.html#the-test-attribute)
and

[,](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html)

`#[divan::bench]``#[divan::bench_group]` functions can
use [:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/testing.html#the-ignore-attribute)

`#[ignore]````
#[divan::bench_group]
#[ignore]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench]
    fn todo() {
        unimplemented!();
    }
}
```
This option can also instead be set within the `#[divan::bench_group]`
attribute:

```
#[divan::bench_group(ignore)]
mod math {
    #[divan::bench]
    fn todo() {
        unimplemented!();
    }
}
```
Like [ skip_ext_time](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time), this option can be set to an explicit

[value to override parent values:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`bool````
#[divan::bench_group(ignore = false)]
mod group {
    // ...
}
```
This can be used to ignore benchmarks based on a runtime condition. The
following example benchmark group will be ignored if an [environment
variable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.var.html) is not set to “true”:

```
#[divan::bench_group(
    ignore = std::env::var("BENCH_EXPENSIVE").as_deref() != Ok("true")
)]
mod expensive_benches {
    // ...
}
```

GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/nvzqz) or [donating via
PayPal](https://paypal.me/nvzqz). Sponsorships help me progress on what’s

[§](https://docs.rs#guide)Guide

A guide is being worked on. In the meantime, see:

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Divan `0.1.21` requires Rust `1.80.0` or later.

-
Add the following to your project’s `Cargo.toml``[dev-dependencies] divan = "0.1.21" [[bench]] name = "example" harness = false`
-
Create a benchmarks file at `benches/example.rs`[1](https://docs.rs#fn1)`fn main() { // Run registered benchmarks. divan::main(); } // Register a `fibonacci` function and benchmark it over multiple cases. #[divan::bench(args = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32])] fn fibonacci(n: u64) -> u64 { if n <= 1 { 1 } else { fibonacci(n - 2) + fibonacci(n - 1) } }`
-
Run your benchmarks with `cargo bench``example fastest │ slowest │ median │ mean │ samples │ iters ╰─ fibonacci │ │ │ │ │ ├─ 1 0.626 ns │ 1.735 ns │ 0.657 ns │ 0.672 ns │ 100 │ 819200 ├─ 2 2.767 ns │ 3.154 ns │ 2.788 ns │ 2.851 ns │ 100 │ 204800 ├─ 4 6.816 ns │ 7.671 ns │ 7.061 ns │ 7.167 ns │ 100 │ 102400 ├─ 8 57.31 ns │ 62.51 ns │ 57.96 ns │ 58.55 ns │ 100 │ 12800 ├─ 16 2.874 µs │ 3.812 µs │ 2.916 µs │ 3.006 µs │ 100 │ 200 ╰─ 32 6.267 ms │ 6.954 ms │ 6.283 ms │ 6.344 ms │ 100 │ 100`

See [ #[divan::bench]](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html) for info on benchmark function registration.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Practical example benchmarks can be found in the [ examples/benches](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/tree/main/examples/benches)
directory. These can be benchmarked locally by running:

```
git clone https://github.com/nvzqz/divan.git
cd divan
cargo bench -q -p examples --all-features
```
More thorough usage examples can be found in the [ #[divan::bench] documentation](https://docs.rs/attr.bench.html#examples).

# condtype 1.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/condtype/^1.3

`condtype`

Choose Rust types at compile-time via boolean constants, brought to you by
[Nikolai Vazquez](https://hachyderm.io/@nikolai).

If you find this library useful, consider
[starring it](https://github.com/nvzqz/condtype) as well as
[sponsoring](https://github.com/sponsors/nvzqz) or
[donating once](https://paypal.me/nvzqz). 💖

## Conditional Typing

The [ CondType](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/type.CondType.html) type and

[macro choose types at compile-time using](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/macro.condval.html)

`condval!`[constants, just like](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

`bool`[. Unlike the](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/conditional)

`std::conditional_t` in C++[type, the type chosen by](https://docs.rs/either/latest/either/enum.Either.html)

`Either`[/](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/type.CondType.html)

`CondType`[is directly used, rather than wrapped with an](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/macro.condval.html)

`condval!`[type. This may be considered a form of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.enum.html)

`enum`[dependent typing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_type), but it is limited in ability and is restricted to compile-time constants rather than runtime values.

`CondType`

In the following example, [ CondType](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/type.CondType.html) aliases either

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[, depending on the boolean](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32`[generic constant](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics):

```
use CondType;
let str:  = "hello";
let int:  = 42;
// Unsized types are also supported:
let str: & = "world";
```
`condval!`

[ condval!](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/macro.condval.html) enables choosing differently-typed values without specifying types.
In the following example,

`val` is inferred to be either [or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[, depending on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32``COND`.```
use condval;
const COND: bool = true;
let val = condval!;
assert_eq!;
```
`if let` pattern matching is also supported:

```
use condval;
const STR:  = Some;
let val = condval!;
assert_eq!;
```
### Platform-Specific Types

This library can make code for some platforms more efficient by using smaller-sized types, depending on platform-specific constants.

In the following example, the `RlimOption` type can be either
[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/enum.Option.html)<[rlim_t](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html)> or [ rlim_t](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html) itself,
where

[can be treated as a sentinel value for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u64.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`rlim_t::MAX`[if it is not equal to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`Option::None`[.](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html)

`RLIM_INFINITY````
use ;
use ;
const RLIM_INFINITY_IS_MAX: bool = RLIM_INFINITY == rlim_tMAX;
type RlimOption = ;
const RLIM_NONE: RlimOption = condval!;
// Convert from either `RlimOption` type to `Option` via the `Into` trait:
let rlim_none:  = RLIM_NONE.into;
```
Without this library, one could otherwise use [ cfg_if!](https://docs.rs/cfg-if/latest/cfg_if/macro.cfg_if.html) to achieve the same
goal. However, using

[requires maintaining a list of platforms and being more fine-grained if](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/attribute/cfg.html)

`#[cfg]`[is dependent on CPU architecture.](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_resource.h.html)

`RLIM_INFINITY````
use cfg_if;
use rlim_t;
cfg_if!
```
## Limitations

It is currently not possible to use [ CondType](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/type.CondType.html) or

[with a](https://docs.rs/condtype/latest/condtype/macro.condval.html)

`condval!`[generic constant](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics)because

[Rust does not yet consider trait implementations based on booleans to be exhaustive](https://github.com/rust-lang/project-const-generics/issues/26). Once that issue is resolved, all versions of this library should

*just work*with generic constants.

```

# regex-lite 0.1.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/regex-lite/^0.1

# regex-lite

This crate provides a **lightweight** regex engine for searching strings. The
regex syntax supported by this crate is nearly identical to what is found in
the `regex` crate. Like the `regex` crate, all regex searches in this crate
have worst case `O(m * n)` time complexity, where `m` is proportional to the
size of the regex and `n` is proportional to the size of the string being
searched.

### Documentation

### Usage

To bring this crate into your repository, either add `regex-lite` to your
`Cargo.toml`, or run `cargo add regex-lite`.

Here's a simple example that matches a date in YYYY-MM-DD format and prints the year, month and day:

```
use Regex;
```
If you have lots of dates in text that you'd like to iterate over, then it's easy to adapt the above example with an iterator:

```
use Regex;
const TO_SEARCH: &'static str = "
On 2010-03-14, foo happened. On 2014-10-14, bar happened.
";
```
This example outputs:

```
year: 2010, month: 03, day: 14
year: 2014, month: 10, day: 14
```
### Minimum Rust version policy

This crate's minimum supported `rustc` version is `1.65.0`.

The policy is that the minimum Rust version required to use this crate can be increased in semver compatible updates.

### Motivation

The primary purpose of this crate is to provide an alternative regex engine
for folks that are unhappy with the binary size and compilation time of the
primary `regex` crate. The `regex-lite` crate does the absolute minimum possible
to act as a drop-in replacement to the `regex` crate's `Regex` type. It avoids
a lot of complexity by choosing not to optimize searches and to opt out of
functionality such as robust Unicode support. By keeping the code simpler
and smaller, we get binary sizes and compile times that are substantially
better than even the `regex` crate with all of its features disabled.

To make the benefits a bit more concrete, here are the results of one
experiment I did. For `regex`, I disabled all features except for `std`:

- `regex 1.7.3`: 1.41s compile time, 373KB relative size increase
- `regex 1.8.1`: 1.46s compile time, 410KB relative size increase
- `regex 1.9.0`: 1.93s compile time, 565KB relative size increase
- `regex-lite 0.1.0`: 0.73s compile time, 94KB relative size increase

The main reason why `regex-lite` does so much better than `regex` when all of
`regex`'s features are disabled is because of irreducible complexity. There are
certain parts of the code in `regex` that can't be arbitrarily divided based
on binary size and compile time goals. It's instead more sustainable to just
maintain an entirely separate crate.

Ideas for improving the binary size and compile times of this crate even more are most welcome.

### License

This project is licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

The data in `regex-syntax/src/unicode_tables/` is licensed under the Unicode
License Agreement
([LICENSE-UNICODE](https://www.unicode.org/copyright.html#License)).

# mimalloc 0.1.52 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/mimalloc/^0.1

# Mimalloc Rust

A drop-in global allocator wrapper around the [mimalloc](https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc) allocator.
Mimalloc is a general purpose, performance oriented allocator built by Microsoft.

## Usage

```
use MiMalloc;
static GLOBAL: MiMalloc = MiMalloc;
```
## Requirements

A **C** compiler is required for building [mimalloc](https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc) with cargo.

## Usage with secure mode

Using secure mode adds guard pages,
randomized allocation, encrypted free lists, etc. The performance penalty is usually
around 10% according to [mimalloc](https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc)
own benchmarks.

To enable secure mode, put in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
mimalloc = { version = "*", features = ["secure"] }
```
## Usage with v2

By default this library uses mimalloc `v3`.
To use MiMalloc `v2`, write in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
mimalloc = { version = "*", features = ["v2"] }
```

# libc 0.2.186 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libc/^0.2.148

# libc - Raw FFI bindings to platforms' system libraries

`libc` provides all of the definitions necessary to easily interoperate with C
code (or "C-like" code) on each of the platforms that Rust supports. This
includes type definitions (e.g. `c_int`), constants (e.g. `EINVAL`) as well as
function headers (e.g. `malloc`).

This crate exports all underlying platform types, functions, and constants under
the crate root, so all items are accessible as `libc::foo`. The types and values
of all the exported APIs match the platform that libc is compiled for.

Windows API bindings are not included in this crate. If you are looking for
WinAPI bindings, consider using crates like [windows-sys](https://docs.rs/windows-sys).

More detailed information about the design of this library can be found in its
[associated RFC](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/HEAD/text/1291-promote-libc.md).

## v1.0 Roadmap

Currently, `libc` has two active branches: `main` for the upcoming v1.0 release,
and `libc-0.2` for the currently published version. By default all pull requests
should target `main`; once reviewed, they can be cherry picked to the `libc-0.2`
branch if needed.

We will stop making new v0.2 releases once v1.0 is released.

See the section in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md#v10-roadmap) for more
details.

## Usage

Add the following to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

-
`std`: by default`libc`links to the standard library. Disable this feature to remove this dependency and be able to use`libc`in`#![no_std]`crates.
-
`extra_traits`: all`struct`s implemented in`libc`are`Copy`and`Clone`. This feature derives`Debug`,`Eq`,`Hash`, and`PartialEq`.

The following features are deprecated:

- `use_std`: this is equivalent to- `std`
- `const-extern-fn`: this is now enabled by default
- `align`: this is now enabled by default

## Rust version support

The minimum supported Rust toolchain version is currently **Rust 1.65**.

Increases to the MSRV are allowed to change without a major (i.e. semver- breaking) release in order to avoid a ripple effect in the ecosystem. A policy for when this may change is a work in progress.

`libc` may continue to compile with Rust versions older than the current MSRV
but this is not guaranteed.

## Platform support

You can see the platform(target)-specific docs on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/libc), select a platform
you want to see.

See [ ci/verify-build.py](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/blob/HEAD/ci/verify-build.py) for
the platforms on which

`libc` is guaranteed to build for each Rust toolchain.
The test matrices at [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/actions)show the platforms in which

`libc` tests
are run.## License

This project is licensed under either of

at your option.

## Contributing

We welcome all people who want to contribute. Please see the
[contributing instructions](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/blob/HEAD/CONTRIBUTING.md) for more information.

Contributions in any form (issues, pull requests, etc.) to this project must
adhere to Rust's [Code of Conduct](https://www.rust-lang.org/policies/code-of-conduct).

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in `libc` by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be
dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# divan 0.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/divan/0.0.0

# Divan

[WIP] Divan (/diːvan/) is a statistically-comfy benchmarking library for Rust
projects, brought to you by [Nikolai Vazquez](https://hachyderm.io/@nikolai).

## License

Like the Rust project, this library may be used under either the
[MIT License](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/blob/main/LICENSE-MIT) or
[Apache License (Version 2.0)](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan/blob/main/LICENSE-APACHE).

# bench in divan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/divan/latest/divan/attr.bench.html

`#[bench]`## Expand description

Registers a benchmarking function.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The quickest way to get started is to benchmark the function as-is:

```
use divan::black_box;
#[divan::bench]
fn add() -> i32 {
    black_box(1) + black_box(42)
}
fn main() {
    // Run `add` benchmark:
    divan::main();
}
```
If benchmarks need to setup context before running, they can take a
[ Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html) and use

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.bench)

`Bencher::bench````
use divan::{Bencher, black_box};
#[divan::bench]
fn copy_from_slice(bencher: Bencher) {
    let src = (0..100).collect::<Vec<i32>>();
    let mut dst = vec![0; src.len()];
    bencher.bench_local(move || {
        black_box(&mut dst).copy_from_slice(black_box(&src));
    });
}
```
Applying this attribute multiple times to the same item will cause a compile error:

[§](https://docs.rs#drop)Drop

When a benchmarked function returns a value, it will not be [dropped](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)
until after the current sample loop is finished. This allows for more
precise timing measurements.

Note that there is an inherent memory cost to defer drop, including
allocations inside not-yet-dropped values. Also, if the benchmark
[panics](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/macro.panic.html), the values will never be dropped.

The following example benchmarks will only measure [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) construction
time, but not deallocation time:

```
use divan::{Bencher, black_box};
#[divan::bench]
fn freestanding() -> String {
    black_box("hello").to_uppercase()
}
#[divan::bench]
fn contextual(bencher: Bencher) {
    // Setup:
    let s: String = // ...
    bencher.bench(|| -> String {
        black_box(&s).to_lowercase()
    });
}
```
If the returned value *does not* need to be dropped, there is no memory
cost. Because of this, the following example benchmarks are equivalent:

```
#[divan::bench]
fn with_return() -> i32 {
    let n: i32 = // ...
    n
}
#[divan::bench]
fn without_return() {
    let n: i32 = // ...
    divan::black_box(n);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#options)Options

- `name`
- `crate`
- `args`
- `consts`
- `types`
- `sample_count`
- `sample_size`
- `threads`
- `counters`
- `min_time`
- `max_time`
- `skip_ext_time`
- `ignore`

[§](https://docs.rs#name)`name`

By default, the benchmark uses the function’s name. It can be overridden via
the [ name](https://docs.rs#name) option:

```
#[divan::bench(name = "my_add")]
fn add() -> i32 {
    // Will appear as "crate_name::my_add".
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate)`crate`

The path to the specific `divan` crate instance used by this macro’s
generated code can be specified via the [ crate](https://docs.rs#crate) option. This is applicable
when using

`divan` via a macro from your own crate.```
extern crate divan as sofa;
#[::sofa::bench(crate = ::sofa)]
fn add() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#args)`args`

Function arguments can be provided to benchmark the function over multiple
cases. This is used for comparing across parameters like collection lengths
and [ enum](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.enum.html) variants. If
you are not comparing cases and just need to pass a value into the
benchmark, instead consider passing local values into the

[closure or use](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.bench)

`Bencher::bench`[for many distinct values.](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html#method.with_inputs)

`Bencher::with_inputs`The following example benchmarks converting a [ Range](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.Range.html) to

[over different lengths:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`Vec````
#[divan::bench(args = [1000, LEN, len()])]
fn init_vec(len: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    (0..len).collect()
}
const LEN: usize = // ...
fn len() -> usize {
    // ...
}
```
The list of arguments can be shared across multiple benchmarks through an
external [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html):

```
const LENS: &[usize] = // ...
#[divan::bench(args = LENS)]
fn bench_vec1(len: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(args = LENS)]
fn bench_vec2(len: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    // ...
}
```
Unlike the [ consts](https://docs.rs#consts) option, any argument type is supported if it
implements

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/any/trait.Any.html)

`Any`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html)

`Copy`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)

`Send`[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html)

`Sync`[(or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html)

`ToString`[):](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html)

`Debug````
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
enum Arg {
    A, B
}
#[divan::bench(args = [Arg::A, Arg::B])]
fn bench_args(arg: Arg) {
    // ...
}
```
The argument type does not need to implement [ Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) if it is used through
a reference:

```
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Arg {
    A, B
}
#[divan::bench(args = [Arg::A, Arg::B])]
fn bench_args(arg: &Arg) {
    // ...
}
```
For convenience, common string types are coerced to [ &str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html):

```
fn strings() -> impl Iterator<Item = String> {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(args = strings())]
fn bench_strings(s: &str) {
    // ...
}
```
Arguments can also be used with [ Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html). This allows for generating
inputs based on

[values or providing throughput information via](https://docs.rs#args)

`args`[:](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html)

`Counter`s```
use divan::Bencher;
#[divan::bench(args = [1, 2, 3])]
fn bench(bencher: Bencher, len: usize) {
    let value = new_value(len);
    bencher
        .counter(len)
        .bench(|| {
            do_work(value);
        });
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#consts)`consts`

Divan supports benchmarking functions with [ const
generics](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics)
via the

[option.](https://docs.rs#consts)

`consts`The following example benchmarks initialization of [ [i32; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)
for values of

`N` provided by a [literal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/literal-expr.html),

[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/constant-items.html)

`const` item[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/const_eval.html#const-functions)

`const fn````
#[divan::bench(consts = [1000, LEN, len()])]
fn init_array<const N: usize>() -> [i32; N] {
    let mut result = [0; N];
    for i in 0..N {
        result[i] = divan::black_box(i as i32);
    }
    result
}
const LEN: usize = // ...
const fn len() -> usize {
    // ...
}
```
The list of constants can be shared across multiple benchmarks through an
external [array](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html) or [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html):

```
const SIZES: &[usize] = &[1, 2, 5, 10];
#[divan::bench(consts = SIZES)]
fn bench_array1<const N: usize>() -> [i32; N] {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(consts = SIZES)]
fn bench_array2<const N: usize>() -> [i32; N] {
    // ...
}
```
External constants are limited to lengths 1 through 20, because of implementation details. This limit does not apply if the list is provided directly like in the first example.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIZES: [usize; 21] = [
    // ...
];
#[divan::bench(consts = SIZES)]
fn bench_array<const N: usize>() -> [i32; N] {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#types)`types`

Divan supports benchmarking generic functions over a list of types via the
[ types](https://docs.rs#types) option.

The following example benchmarks the [ From<&str>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html) implementations
for

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````
#[divan::bench(types = [&str, String])]
fn from_str<'a, T>() -> T
where
    T: From<&'a str>,
{
    divan::black_box("hello world").into()
}
```
The [ types](https://docs.rs#types) and

[options can be combined to benchmark](https://docs.rs#args)

`args`*T*×

*A*scenarios. The following example benchmarks the

[implementations for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.FromIterator.html)

`FromIterator`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`Vec`[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/set/struct.BTreeSet.html)

`BTreeSet`[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)

`HashSet````
use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashSet};
#[divan::bench(
    types = [Vec<i32>, BTreeSet<i32>, HashSet<i32>],
    args = [0, 2, 4, 16, 256, 4096],
)]
fn from_range<T>(n: i32) -> T
where
    T: FromIterator<i32>,
{
    (0..n).collect()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#sample_count)`sample_count`

The number of statistical sample recordings can be set to a predetermined
[ u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) value via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#sample_count)

`sample_count``DIVAN_SAMPLE_COUNT` environment variable or
`--sample-count` CLI argument.```
#[divan::bench(sample_count = 1000)]
fn add() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
If the [ threads](https://docs.rs#threads) option is enabled, sample count becomes a multiple of the
number of threads. This is because each thread operates over the same sample
size to ensure there are always N competing threads doing the same amount of
work.

[§](https://docs.rs#sample_size)`sample_size`

The number iterations within each statistics sample can be set to a
predetermined [ u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) value via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#sample_size)

`sample_size``DIVAN_SAMPLE_SIZE` environment
variable or `--sample-size` CLI argument.```
#[divan::bench(sample_size = 1000)]
fn add() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#threads)`threads`

Benchmarked functions can be run across multiple threads via the [ threads](https://docs.rs#threads)
option. This enables you to measure contention on

[atomics and locks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/index.html). The default thread count is the

[available parallelism](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/thread/functions/fn.available_parallelism.html).

```
use std::sync::Arc;
#[divan::bench(threads)]
fn arc_clone(bencher: divan::Bencher) {
    let arc = Arc::new(42);
    bencher.bench(|| arc.clone());
}
```
The [ threads](https://docs.rs#threads) option can be set to any of:

- `bool`- [available parallelism](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/thread/functions/fn.available_parallelism.html)(true) or no parallelism.
- `usize`- [available parallelism](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/thread/functions/fn.available_parallelism.html)and 1 means no parallelism.
- `IntoIterator`- `usize`

```
#[divan::bench(threads = false)]
fn single() {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(threads = 10)]
fn specific() {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(threads = 0..=8)]
fn range() {
    // Note: Includes 0 for available parallelism.
}
#[divan::bench(threads = [0, 1, 4, 8, 16])]
fn selection() {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#counters)`counters`

The [ Counters](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html) of each iteration can be set via
the

[option. The following example emits info for the number of bytes and number of ints processed when benchmarking](https://docs.rs#counters)

`counters`[slice sorting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.sort):

```
use divan::{Bencher, counter::{BytesCount, ItemsCount}};
const INTS: &[i32] = &[
    // ...
];
#[divan::bench(counters = [
    BytesCount::of_slice(INTS),
    ItemsCount::new(INTS.len()),
])]
fn sort(bencher: Bencher) {
    bencher
        .with_inputs(|| INTS.to_vec())
        .bench_refs(|ints| ints.sort());
}
```
For convenience, singular `counter` allows a single
[ Counter](https://docs.rs/counter/trait.Counter.html) to be set. The following example emits
info for the number of bytes processed when benchmarking

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.Chars.html#method.count)

`char`-counting```
use divan::counter::BytesCount;
const STR: &str = "...";
#[divan::bench(counter = BytesCount::of_str(STR))]
fn char_count() -> usize {
    divan::black_box(STR).chars().count()
}
```
See:

[§](https://docs.rs#bytes_count)`bytes_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [BytesCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.BytesCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#chars_count)`chars_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [CharsCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.CharsCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#items_count)`items_count`

Convenience shorthand for
[counter](https://docs.rs#counters) = [ItemsCount](https://docs.rs/counter/struct.ItemsCount.html)::from(n)

[§](https://docs.rs#min_time)`min_time`

The minimum time spent benchmarking each function can be set to a
predetermined [ Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html) via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#min_time)

`min_time``DIVAN_MIN_TIME` environment variable
or `--min-time` CLI argument.Unless [ skip_ext_time](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time) is set, this includes time external to the
benchmarked function, such as time spent generating inputs and running

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop````
use std::time::Duration;
#[divan::bench(min_time = Duration::from_secs(3))]
fn add() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
For convenience, [ min_time](https://docs.rs#min_time) can also be set with seconds as

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)

`u64`[. Invalid values will cause a panic at runtime.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64````
#[divan::bench(min_time = 2)]
fn int_secs() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(min_time = 1.5)]
fn float_secs() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#max_time)`max_time`

The maximum time spent benchmarking each function can be set to a
predetermined [ Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html) via the

[option. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#max_time)

`max_time``DIVAN_MAX_TIME` environment variable
or `--max-time` CLI argument.Unless [ skip_ext_time](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time) is set, this includes time external to the
benchmarked function, such as time spent generating inputs and running

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`If `min_time > max_time`, then [ max_time](https://docs.rs#max_time) has priority and

[will not be reached.](https://docs.rs#min_time)

`min_time````
use std::time::Duration;
#[divan::bench(max_time = Duration::from_secs(5))]
fn add() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
For convenience, like [ min_time](https://docs.rs#min_time),

[can also be set with seconds as](https://docs.rs#max_time)

`max_time`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)

`u64`[. Invalid values will cause a panic at runtime.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64````
#[divan::bench(max_time = 8)]
fn int_secs() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
#[divan::bench(max_time = 9.5)]
fn float_secs() -> i32 {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time)`skip_ext_time`

By default, [ min_time](https://docs.rs#min_time) and

[include time external to the benchmarked function, such as time spent generating inputs and running](https://docs.rs#max_time)

`max_time`[. Enabling the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[option will instead make those options only consider time spent within the benchmarked function. This may be overridden at runtime using either the](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time)

`skip_ext_time``DIVAN_SKIP_EXT_TIME` environment
variable or `--skip-ext-time` CLI argument.In the following example, [ max_time](https://docs.rs#max_time) only considers time spent running

`measured_function`:```
#[divan::bench(max_time = 5, skip_ext_time)]
fn bench(bencher: divan::Bencher) {
    bencher
        .with_inputs(|| generate_input())
        .bench_values(|input| measured_function(input));
}
```
This option can be set to an explicit [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) value to override parent
values:

```
#[divan::bench(max_time = 5, skip_ext_time = false)]
fn bench(bencher: divan::Bencher) {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#ignore)`ignore`

Like [ #[test]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/testing.html#the-test-attribute),

`#[divan::bench]` functions can use [:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/testing.html#the-ignore-attribute)

`#[ignore]````
#[divan::bench]
#[ignore]
fn todo() {
    unimplemented!();
}
```
This option can also instead be set within the `#[divan::bench]` attribute:

```
#[divan::bench(ignore)]
fn todo() {
    unimplemented!();
}
```
Like [ skip_ext_time](https://docs.rs#skip_ext_time), this option can be set to an explicit

[value to override parent values:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`bool````
#[divan::bench(ignore = false)]
fn bench() {
    // ...
}
```
This can be used to ignore benchmarks based on a runtime condition. The
following example benchmark will be ignored if an [environment
variable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.var.html) is not set to “true”:

```
#[divan::bench(
    ignore = std::env::var("BENCH_EXPENSIVE").as_deref() != Ok("true")
)]
fn expensive_bench() {
    // ...
}
```

    example       fastest  │ slowest  │ median   │ mean     │ samples │ iters

       ├─ 1       0.626 ns │ 1.735 ns │ 0.657 ns │ 0.672 ns │ 100     │ 819200

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cfg-if/1.0.4/target-redirect/cfg_if/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

# cfg_if in cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1/macro.cfg_if.html

```
macro_rules! cfg_if {
    (
        if #[cfg( $($i_meta:tt)+ )] { $( $i_tokens:tt )* }
        $(
            else if #[cfg( $($ei_meta:tt)+ )] { $( $ei_tokens:tt )* }
        )*
        $(
            else { $( $e_tokens:tt )* }
        )?
    ) => { ... };
    (@__items ( $( ($($_:tt)*) , )* ) ; ) => { ... };
    (
        @__items ( $( ($($no:tt)+) , )* ) ;
        (( $( $($yes:tt)+ )? ) ( $( $tokens:tt )* )),
        $( $rest:tt , )*
    ) => { ... };
    (@__temp_group $( $tokens:tt )* ) => { ... };
}
```

The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

# automod - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/automod/^1.0.16/

## Expand description

**Pull in every source file in a directory as a module.**

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

`automod::dir!("path/to/directory");`This macro expands to one or more `mod` items, one for each source file in
the specified directory, excluding `mod.rs`, `lib.rs`, and `main.rs`.

The path is given relative to the directory containing Cargo.toml.

It is an error if the given directory contains no source files or if a file name is not valid UTF-8.

The macro takes an optional visibility to apply on the generated modules:
`automod::dir!(pub "path/to/directory")`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Suppose that we would like to keep a directory of regression tests for individual numbered issues:

- tests/
- regression/
- issue1.rs
- issue2.rs
- …
- issue128.rs

- regression/

We would like to be able to toss files in this directory and have them
automatically tested, without listing them in some explicit list of modules.
Automod solves this by adding *tests/regression.rs* containing:

```
mod regression {
    automod::dir!("tests/regression");
}
```
The macro invocation expands to:

```
mod issue1;
mod issue2;
/* ... */
mod issue128;
```

# jiff - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jiff/^0.2.23/

## Expand description

Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. The focus of this library is providing high level datetime primitives that are difficult to misuse and have reasonable performance.

Jiff takes enormous inspiration from [Temporal](https://tc39.es/proposal-temporal/docs/index.html), which is a [TC39](https://tc39.es/) proposal to
improve datetime handling in JavaScript.

Here is a quick example that shows how to parse a typical RFC 3339 instant, convert it to a zone aware datetime, add a span of time and losslessly print it:

```
use jiff::{Timestamp, ToSpan};
let time: Timestamp = "2024-07-11T01:14:00Z".parse()?;
let zoned = time.in_tz("America/New_York")?.checked_add(1.month().hours(2))?;
assert_eq!(zoned.to_string(), "2024-08-10T23:14:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
// Or, if you want an RFC3339 formatted string:
assert_eq!(zoned.timestamp().to_string(), "2024-08-11T03:14:00Z");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

The primary type in this crate is [ Zoned](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html). A

`Zoned` value is a datetime that
corresponds to a precise instant in time in a particular geographic region.
Users of this crate may find it helpful to think of a `Zoned` as a triple of
the following components:- A `Timestamp`[Unix epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time). A timestamp is a precise instant in time.
- A `civil::DateTime`
- A `tz::TimeZone`[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time), in a particular geographic region.

All three of these components are used to provide convenient high level
operations on `Zoned` such as computing durations, adding durations and
rounding.

A [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) is this crate’s primary duration type. It mixes calendar and clock
units into a single type. Jiff also provides

[, which is like](https://docs.rs/struct.SignedDuration.html)

`SignedDuration`[, but signed. Users should default to a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`std::time::Duration``Span` for
representing durations when using Jiff.The remainder of this documentation is organized as follows:

- [Features](https://docs.rs#features)gives a very brief summary of the features Jiff does and does not support.
- [Usage](https://docs.rs#usage)shows how to add Jiff to your Rust project.
- [Examples](https://docs.rs#examples)shows a small cookbook of programs for common tasks.
- [Crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features)documents the Cargo features that can be enabled or disabled for this crate.

Also, the `_documentation` sub-module serves to provide longer form
documentation:

- [Comparison with other Rust datetime crates](https://docs.rs/_documentation/comparison/index.html)
- [The API design rationale for Jiff](https://docs.rs/_documentation/design/index.html)
- [Platform support](https://docs.rs/_documentation/platform/index.html)
- [CHANGELOG](https://docs.rs/_documentation/changelog/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Here is a non-exhaustive list of the things that Jiff supports:

- Automatic and seamless integration with your system’s copy of the
[IANA Time Zone Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tz_database). When a platform doesn’t have a time zone database, Jiff automatically embeds a copy of it.
- A separation of datetime types between absolute times (`Timestamp``Zoned``civil::DateTime`
- Nanosecond precision.
- Time zone and daylight saving time aware arithmetic.
- The primary duration type, `Span`
- An “absolute” duration type, `SignedDuration``std::time::Duration`
- Datetime rounding.
- Span rounding, including calendar units and including taking time zones into account.
- Formatting and parsing datetimes via a Temporal-specified hybrid format
that takes the best parts of [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339),[RFC 9557](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9557.html)and[ISO 8601](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html). This includes lossless round tripping of zone aware datetimes and durations.
- Formatting and parsing according to [RFC 2822](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2822).
- Formatting and parsing via routines similar to `strftime``strptime`
- Formatting and parsing durations via a bespoke
[“friendly” format](https://docs.rs/fmt/friendly/index.html), with Serde support, that is meant to service the`humantime`
- Opt-in Serde integration.
- Full support for dealing with ambiguous civil datetimes.
- Protection against deserializing datetimes in the future with an offset
different than what is possible with your copy of the Time Zone Database.
(This is done via `tz::OffsetConflict`
- APIs that panic by design are clearly documented as such and few in number.
Otherwise, all operations that can fail, including because of overflow,
return a `Result`.

Here is also a list of things that Jiff doesn’t currently support, along with a link to a relevant issue (if one exists).

- [Leap seconds](https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/7). (Jiff will automatically constrain times like- `23:59:60`to- `23:59:59`.)
- Time scales other than Unix.
- [Calendars other than Gregorian](https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/6).
- [Localization](https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/4).
- [Changing the representation size, precision or limits on the minimum and maximum datetime values.](https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/3)
- [Jiff aims to have reasonable performance and may not be capable of doing the fastest possible thing.](https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/17)

At present, it is recommended to use the [ icu](https://docs.rs/icu) crate via

[for localization and non-Gregorian use cases.](https://docs.rs/jiff-icu)

`jiff-icu`Please file an issue if you can think of more (substantial) things to add to the above list.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Jiff is [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/jiff) and can be
used by adding `jiff` to your dependencies in your project’s `Cargo.toml`.
Or more simply, just run `cargo add jiff`.

Here is a complete example that creates a new Rust project, adds a dependency
on `jiff`, creates the source code for a simple datetime program and then runs
it.

First, create the project in a new directory:

```
$ cargo new jiff-example
$ cd jiff-example
```
Second, add a dependency on `jiff`:

`$ cargo add jiff`Third, edit `src/main.rs`. Delete what’s there and replace it with this:

```
use jiff::{Unit, Zoned};
fn main() -> Result<(), jiff::Error> {
    let now = Zoned::now().round(Unit::Second)?;
    println!("{now}");
    Ok(())
}
```
Fourth, run it with `cargo run`:

```
$ cargo run
   Compiling jiff v0.2.0 (/home/andrew/rust/jiff)
   Compiling jiff-play v0.2.0 (/home/andrew/tmp/scratch/rust/jiff-play)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1.37s
     Running `target/debug/jiff-play`
2024-07-10T19:54:20-04:00[America/New_York]
```
The first time you run the program will show more output like above. But subsequent runs shouldn’t have to re-compile the dependencies.
